analysis.one_liner: Bans using medically important antibiotics in livestock feed unless proven safe for human health.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced by Rep. Sherrod Brown with 10 Democratic cosponsors, never got a vote: it sat in a House committee and its subcommittee for the rest of the Congress and expired in January 2001.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have barred the routine, low-dose use of antibiotics like penicillin and tetracycline in livestock feed — used mainly to make animals grow faster — unless the Health and Human Services Secretary found a reasonable certainty of no harm to people from antibiotic-resistant bacteria. Existing approvals would have been withdrawn within two years unless the drug makers proved safety. The bill never left committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people who rely on antibiotics to treat infections like salmonella, campylobacter, and E. coli illness. The bill's findings cite government and international studies linking livestock antibiotic use to resistant bacteria that can infect people, and it would have preserved the effectiveness of essential human medicines.

how_it_helps.text: The bill would prohibit subtherapeutic use of essential antibiotics in animal feed unless the HHS Secretary determines a reasonable certainty of no human health threat from antimicrobial resistance.

Existing approvals for subtherapeutic use of penicillin, tetracycline, erythromycin, lincomycin, tylosin, bacitracin, virginiamycin, and similar drugs would be withdrawn within two years unless manufacturers submitted data proving no harm to human health.

The bill cites the National Academy of Sciences, the World Health Organization, the European Union, and a 1999 GAO study finding that resistant salmonella, campylobacter, and E. coli in humans are linked to antibiotic use in animals.
Animals that are actually sick would still be treated: the bill defines subtherapeutic use to exclude high-level, short-term treatment of ill animals.

analysis.who_pays: Livestock producers, who would lose growth-promotion antibiotics and might face slightly higher production costs, and the animal-drug companies that sell feed-additive antibiotics, which would lose those sales unless they proved safety within two years.

drawbacks.text: The bill would withdraw existing approvals within two years unless manufacturers produced safety data, a short window that would force quick changes in feeding practices across the livestock industry.

Livestock producers could face higher production costs from switching to alternative growth promoters or husbandry practices; the bill's own findings acknowledge the change, asserting that non-antibiotic alternatives exist and would not hinder livestock raising.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main benefit — keeping essential antibiotics effective against life-threatening infections — protects everyone, and the bill left treatment of genuinely sick animals untouched. The main cost falls on livestock producers and feed-drug makers in the form of changed practices and lost growth-promotion sales, with some possibility of modestly higher meat prices. On the bill's own record, the public-health benefit outweighed the industry cost.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Commerce Committee, then to its Health and Environment Subcommittee, where it sat until the Congress ended in January 2001 — no hearing, no markup, no vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Sherrod Brown of Ohio introduced the bill on November 9, 1999, joined by Reps. Henry Waxman and Louise Slaughter.
The House referred it to the Committee on Commerce the day it was introduced.
On November 17, 1999, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health and Environment; no further action was ever recorded.
The bill had 10 cosponsors, all Democrats, and the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001 with the bill still in subcommittee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Livestock producers and the makers of growth-promotion antibiotic feed additives avoided new restrictions and kept their existing sales; antibiotic resistance risks were left unaddressed.

for.name: Sherrod Brown
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill to require proof of safety before essential antibiotics could be used in livestock feed.

against.name: House Commerce Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, controlled by Republicans
against.what_they_did: Received the bill and referred it to the Health and Environment Subcommittee; no hearing, markup, or floor vote was ever scheduled.

against.name: Livestock and animal-drug industry
against.role: Feed-additive antibiotic sellers and their producer customers
against.what_they_did: Opposed restrictions on antibiotic growth promoters in livestock feed, an interest that was well protected by the bill never advancing.

sides.party_line_note: There was no vote, so no party split was recorded; all 11 sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats, and the bill died in a committee controlled by the Republican majority without any recorded opposition or support.

industries.note: The bill would have taken away routine low-dose antibiotics used to speed growth, forcing changes in feeding and husbandry practices that could raise production costs slightly. Their interest ran against the public's interest in keeping antibiotics effective.

Companies selling penicillin, tetracycline, and similar feed additives would have lost the growth-promotion market unless they proved safety within two years. Their revenue depended on a use that the bill's findings say endangers human health.
